# Non-Congruence Veech Groups of Origamis

## Main Result

This work establishes a fundamental result concerning the arithmetic properties of Veech groups associated to translation surfaces. Specifically, we demonstrate that **for every genus $g > 1$, there exists a translation surface whose Veech group is a non-congruence subgroup of $SL(2,\mathbb{Z})$**. This result addresses a natural question in the theory of translation surfaces and their associated Teichmüller curves: while it has long been known that Veech groups of origamis are commensurable with $SL(2,\mathbb{Z})$ and hence arithmetic, the finer question of whether these groups satisfy the stronger congruence condition had remained open in general. Our construction provides explicit counterexamples across all relevant genera, showing that non-congruence behavior is not an isolated phenomenon but occurs systematically as the genus varies.

The examples that substantiate this theorem are built using **origamis**, also known as **square-tiled surfaces**. These combinatorial objects provide a particularly tractable class of translation surfaces: they are constructed by gluing finitely many unit squares according to prescribed edge identifications, yielding a translation surface with a canonical structure. Origamis are especially well-suited to computational investigation of Veech groups because their associated Teichmüller curves are defined over $\mathbb{Q}$, and their Veech groups can be described combinatorially in terms of the permutations governing the horizontal and vertical gluing patterns. This combinatorial accessibility makes origamis an ideal testing ground for questions about the arithmetic nature of Veech groups, as it allows explicit computation and verification of non-congruence phenomena that might otherwise remain purely existential.

## Structure of the Article

### Part One: Foundations

The first part of the article is devoted to establishing the foundational framework necessary for the subsequent constructions and proofs. We introduce the basic theory of **translation surfaces**, recalling their definition as Riemann surfaces equipped with an atlas of charts to $\mathbb{C}$ whose transition maps are translations, together with the associated flat geometric structure this induces. We then specialize to **origamis**, detailing their construction from square gluings and explaining how the combinatorial data of an origami (encoded via a pair of permutations) determines the underlying translation surface.

Building on this, we review the theory of **Veech groups**, which arise as the image in $PSL(2,\mathbb{R})$ of the stabilizer of a translation surface under the natural $GL^+(2,\mathbb{R})$-action, and we discuss the associated **Teichmüller curves**, which are obtained as the image of the corresponding $SL(2,\mathbb{R})$-orbit in the moduli space of curves. These Teichmüller curves provide the geometric context in which the arithmetic properties of Veech groups become meaningful, since the Veech group of an origami is by construction a finite-index subgroup of $SL(2,\mathbb{Z})$.

As a concrete illustration of the phenomena investigated in this article, the first part concludes by exhibiting **two explicit origamis in genus 2** whose Veech groups are shown to be non-congruence subgroups of $SL(2,\mathbb{Z})$. These examples serve a dual purpose: they provide the base cases for the low-genus setting and demonstrate, through direct and explicit computation, the general strategy that will later be generalized. The techniques used to verify the non-congruence property for these two origamis—typically involving the computation of the index and level of the Veech group and comparing these invariants against the constraints imposed by congruence subgroups—illustrate concretely how such phenomena can be detected and confirmed.

### Part Two: General Construction and Proof

The second part of the article develops the technical machinery required to extend the genus 2 examples to arbitrary genus $g > 1$. The central contribution here is a **systematic technique for generating sequences of origamis whose Veech groups form a strictly decreasing chain** of subgroups of $SL(2,\mathbb{Z})$. This construction proceeds by successively modifying a given origami—typically through operations such as covering constructions, square subdivisions, or controlled gluing modifications—in a manner that allows precise tracking of how the corresponding Veech group changes at each stage.

This inductive or iterative technique is central to the paper's strategy, as it transforms the problem of finding non-congruence examples in every genus into a problem of controlling how Veech groups behave under these origami-theoretic operations. By carefully analyzing the effect of each step in the sequence on the associated Veech group, we are able to guarantee that non-congruence behavior, once established at some stage, persists (or can be suitably re-established) as the construction proceeds.

Finally, this technique is applied to **prove the main result in full generality**: by starting from the genus 2 examples established in the first part and applying the decreasing sequence construction, we produce, for every genus $g > 1$, an explicit origami whose Veech group fails to be a congruence subgroup of $SL(2,\mathbb{Z})$. This completes the proof of the main theorem and demonstrates that the phenomenon of non-congruence Veech groups is a robust and pervasive feature of the theory of translation surfaces, rather than a peculiarity confined to a small number of low-genus examples.

# Translation Surfaces, Origamis, and Non-Congruence Veech Groups

## Introduction

A translation surface is a Riemann surface equipped with a flat metric with isolated conical singularities, obtained by gluing together polygons in the plane along parallel sides via translations. Associated to every translation surface $X$ is its **Veech group** $\Gamma(X) \subset \mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbb{R})$, the stabilizer of $X$ under the natural action of $\mathrm{GL}^+(2,\mathbb{R})$ on the moduli space of translation surfaces (post-composed with an affine deformation). This group encodes the affine symmetries of the surface and controls essential dynamical properties of the associated billiard or interval exchange transformation, most notably through the dichotomy of Veech: if $\Gamma(X)$ is a lattice in $\mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbb{R})$, then the straight-line flow on $X$ is uniquely ergodic in every irrational direction.

Among the richest and most tractable sources of examples are the **origamis**, also known as **square-tiled surfaces**. An origami is a translation surface obtained by gluing together finitely many unit squares edge-to-edge according to combinatorial gluing rules encoded by a pair of permutations, or equivalently by a finite-index subgroup of the free group $F_2$, or by a covering of the torus branched only over one point. Origamis form a dense (in fact, integral-point) subset of every stratum of the moduli space of translation surfaces, and their Veech groups are automatically arithmetic: they are always commensurable with $\mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbb{Z})$, in fact they are finite-index subgroups of $\mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbb{Z})$ itself. This arithmeticity makes origamis an ideal combinatorial testing ground for questions about the possible shapes that Veech groups can take.

A natural and long-standing question, motivated by analogy with the theory of modular curves, asks whether the Veech groups arising from origamis are always **congruence subgroups** of $\mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbb{Z})$ — that is, whether they always contain a principal congruence subgroup $\Gamma(N)$ as the *full* preimage of some subgroup of $\mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z})$, in the sense familiar from the classical theory of modular forms. Early computations of Veech groups for small, symmetric origamis tended to produce congruence examples, which lent some initial plausibility to a positive answer. However, congruence behavior is far from automatic: the combinatorics of the permutations defining an origami can conspire to produce a Veech group that, while still a finite-index subgroup of $\mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbb{Z})$, fails to be defined by any congruence condition modulo $N$.

## Contents and Methods

This paper addresses precisely this question. Building on the combinatorial and group-theoretic description of origamis in terms of pairs of permutations (or equivalently, subgroups of $F_2$), we develop a systematic method for constructing origamis whose Veech groups can be controlled and, crucially, made to shrink along a sequence of related surfaces. The core technical tool is a construction that takes an origami $\mathcal{O}$ and produces from it a new origami $\mathcal{O}'$, of strictly larger degree, whose Veech group is a proper subgroup of $\Gamma(\mathcal{O})$. Iterating this construction yields an infinite sequence of origamis
$$
\mathcal{O}_0 \;\rightsquigarrow\; \mathcal{O}_1 \;\rightsquigarrow\; \mathcal{O}_2 \;\rightsquigarrow\; \cdots
$$
with a corresponding strictly decreasing chain of Veech groups
$$
\Gamma(\mathcal{O}_0) \supsetneq \Gamma(\mathcal{O}_1) \supsetneq \Gamma(\mathcal{O}_2) \supsetneq \cdots,
$$
all sitting inside $\mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbb{Z})$. This construction is flexible enough to be applied within a fixed genus stratum, or to be adapted so as to control the genus of the resulting surfaces at each stage, which is essential for producing examples across all genera.

The decreasing-sequence technique is of independent interest, since it provides a mechanism for generating large families of origamis with prescribed containment relations among their Veech groups, and it can in principle be used to probe other structural questions about the subgroup lattice of $\mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbb{Z})$ realized by origami Veech groups.

## Main Results

The central result of the paper is the following:

**Theorem.** For every genus $g > 1$, there exists a translation surface of genus $g$ whose Veech group is a **non-congruence** finite-index subgroup of $\mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbb{Z})$.

The proof proceeds in two stages. First, we exhibit **two explicit origamis of genus 2**, given concretely by pairs of permutations on a small number of squares, and compute their Veech groups directly using the standard algorithm for origami Veech groups (via the associated finite-index subgroup and its action on the coset graph, together with an analysis of the cusp widths and elliptic points). In both examples, a direct check — comparing the trace field data, the cusp widths, or the index and generators of the group against the classification of congruence subgroups of a given level and index — shows that the resulting Veech group cannot arise from any congruence condition modulo $N$ for any $N$. These two genus-2 examples thus already establish the theorem in the base case $g = 2$.

Second, to extend the result to arbitrary genus $g > 1$, we apply the decreasing-sequence construction developed earlier in the paper, starting from one of the genus-2 non-congruence examples and iterating the construction while simultaneously tracking and adjusting the genus of the resulting origami at each step. Since the Veech group of each surface in the sequence is contained in the Veech group of its predecessor, and since the initial surface's Veech group is already non-congruence, a group-theoretic argument shows that non-congruence behavior is inherited (or can be arranged to persist) along the sequence: the resulting Veech groups in higher genus remain non-congruence subgroups of $\mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbb{Z})$. This yields the desired examples in every genus $g > 1$, completing the proof of the theorem.

## Significance

This work settles, in the negative, the question of whether Veech groups of translation surfaces — even those arising from the highly structured and arithmetic class of origamis — are necessarily congruence subgroups. The result shows that the analogy between Veech groups and the classical congruence subgroups of modular curve theory breaks down in general, and it does so uniformly across all genera greater than one. Beyond the specific theorem, the sequence-construction technique introduced here offers a reusable tool for future investigations into the structure of origami Veech groups, their commensurability classes, and their distribution within the subgroup lattice of $\mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbb{Z})$.

# Veech and Teichmüller Theory

The mathematician William A. Veech made profound contributions to the study of Teichmüller theory, a field that sits at the intersection of complex analysis, hyperbolic geometry, and dynamical systems. Teichmüller space itself, named after Oswald Teichmüller, parametrizes the different complex structures that can be placed on a given topological surface. Understanding the geometry of this space—and the dynamics that occur upon it—has become a central theme in modern geometric analysis.

Veech's most celebrated contribution is the concept now known as a **Veech surface**, a translation surface whose Veech group (the stabilizer of the surface under the natural action of SL(2,ℝ) on the space of translation surfaces) is a lattice in SL(2,ℝ). This discovery, made in the late 1980s, revealed a remarkable rigidity phenomenon: for these special surfaces, the dynamics of straight-line flows are completely understood, following what is now called the **Veech dichotomy**. Every direction on a Veech surface is either periodic (all trajectories are closed) or uniquely ergodic (trajectories equidistribute).

This work connected deeply to the broader study of the moduli space of Riemann surfaces, since Teichmüller space serves as the universal cover of moduli space. The SL(2,ℝ) action Veech studied is intimately related to the **Teichmüller geodesic flow**, a natural flow on the moduli space of translation surfaces (or equivalently, on the moduli space of quadratic differentials) that generalizes the geodesic flow on hyperbolic surfaces. Veech's insights helped establish that certain orbits of this flow—corresponding to lattice surfaces—behave with exceptional regularity, in stark contrast to the generic chaotic behavior predicted by ergodic theory.

The influence of Veech's ideas extends across several major developments:

- **Interval exchange transformations**: Veech's work provided crucial tools for understanding the dynamics of interval exchange maps, showing connections to unique ergodicity and the Keane conjecture.

- **The Veech alternative**: This dichotomy has inspired the search for other lattice surfaces and their classification, leading to rich examples such as the regular octagon translation surface.

- **Ratner-type rigidity**: Veech's results anticipated later, more general rigidity theorems in the field, particularly the celebrated work of Eskin-Mirzakhani-Mohammadi, which established measure and orbit classification results for the SL(2,ℝ) action on strata of translation surfaces—directly building upon the foundational examples and phenomena that Veech first identified.

Today, the study of Veech groups and Veech surfaces remains an active area of research, forming a bridge between the classical theory of Teichmüller spaces and contemporary work in homogeneous dynamics. The interplay between algebraic structure (the Veech group as a Fuchsian group), geometric structure (the translation surface), and dynamical behavior (flow trajectories) exemplifies the deep unity that Teichmüller theory brings to seemingly disparate areas of mathematics.

# Square-Tiled Surfaces and Non-Congruence Veech Groups

## Overview

This summary addresses research establishing that **non-congruence subgroups arise as Veech groups of square-tiled surfaces in every genus**. This resolves a natural question about the arithmetic nature of Veech groups across all genera of Riemann surfaces.

## Background Concepts

**Square-tiled surfaces** (also called origamis) are translation surfaces obtained by gluing finitely many unit squares edge-to-edge according to combinatorial rules. They form a countable, dense subset of the moduli space of translation surfaces and correspond precisely to points on Riemann surfaces defined over the rationals (via the Belyi-type correspondence with the action of the absolute Galois group).

**Veech groups** are the subgroups of SL(2,ℤ) (or PSL(2,ℤ)) that stabilize a given translation surface under the natural action of SL(2,ℝ). For square-tiled surfaces, the Veech group is always a finite-index subgroup of SL(2,ℤ), since these surfaces correspond to finite covers of the torus branched over one point.

**Congruence subgroups** are those finite-index subgroups of SL(2,ℤ) that contain a principal congruence subgroup Γ(N) for some N. Not every finite-index subgroup is congruence—the existence of **non-congruence subgroups** is a classical phenomenon in the theory of Fuchsian groups.

## Key Result

The central result of this line of research demonstrates:

> **For every genus g ≥ 1 (or g ≥ 2, depending on the precise formulation), there exist square-tiled surfaces whose Veech group is a non-congruence subgroup of SL(2,ℤ).**

This is significant because:
1. Early known examples of Veech groups (e.g., from Weierstrass curves, or surfaces with small numbers of squares) were often congruence subgroups, leading to speculation about whether this might be a general pattern.
2. Establishing non-congruence examples in *every* genus shows this phenomenon is not confined to sporadic low-genus cases but is a robust, generic feature of the theory.

## Methods

Typical strategies employed in such results include:

- **Explicit combinatorial constructions**: Building specific square-tiled surfaces (specifying permutation pairs generating a transitive subgroup of S_n, defining the horizontal and vertical gluing) and computing their Veech groups directly via the associated **origami curve** and its stabilizer.

- **Covering constructions**: Taking a known non-congruence example in low genus and constructing branched or unbranched covers to propagate non-congruence Veech groups to higher genus while controlling how the Veech group transforms under covering.

- **Index and trace computations**: Using the classification of finite-index subgroups of SL(2,ℤ) via their action on cosets (permutation representations), and checking failure of the congruence property by examining whether the subgroup contains the full principal congruence subgroup Γ(N) for the appropriate level N (often detected via the **congruence subgroup test**: comparing the group generated by parabolic/elliptic elements against SL(2,ℤ/Nℤ)).

- **Teichmüller curve perspective**: Since the Veech group determines (up to finite index issues) the **Teichmüller curve** traced out by the SL(2,ℝ)-orbit of the square-tiled surface in moduli space, non-congruence Veech groups correspond to Teichmüller curves whose associated cover of the modular curve is *not* a standard modular curve X(N), X_0(N), or X_1(N).

## Significance

- **Number-theoretic consequences**: Non-congruence subgroups have associated modular forms that don't fit into the classical Hecke theory in the same way, connecting to deep questions about Galois representations attached to non-congruence modular forms (à la Scholl).

- **Dynamics on moduli space**: The result illustrates the richness and complexity of the SL(2,ℝ)-orbit closures (Teichmüller dynamics) beyond the well-understood Veech surfaces coming from Weierstrass curves or Hilbert modular surfaces, whose Veech groups are typically congruence or arithmetic in a classical sense.

- **Galois action**: Since square-tiled surfaces are defined over ℚ̄, the absolute Galois group acts on them; understanding which Veech groups arise (congruence vs. non-congruence) sheds light on the arithmetic geometry of the corresponding origami curves and their Galois orbits.

## Conclusion

This body of work confirms that non-congruence phenomena are ubiquitous rather than exceptional in the study of Veech groups of square-tiled surfaces, holding in every genus. This enriches the connection between flat geometry/Teichmüller dynamics and the classical theory of modular curves and non-congruence subgroups of SL(2,ℤ).

# Abstract

We investigate the arithmetic and geometric structure of Veech groups arising from origami curves (square-tiled surfaces) and demonstrate that non-congruence subgroups of $SL(2,\mathbb{Z})$ occur naturally as Veech groups of translation surfaces in every genus $g > 1$. An origami, or square-tiled surface, is constructed by taking a finite collection of unit squares and gluing their edges according to a pair of permutations $(\sigma, \tau) \in S_n \times S_n$ satisfying a transitivity condition; this data endows the resulting surface with a translation structure and a natural covering map to the standard torus branched only over the origin. The associated Veech group—the stabilizer in $SL(2,\mathbb{Z})$ of the corresponding point in Teichmüller space—is a finite-index subgroup, and the central question is whether it arises as a congruence subgroup.

We show that by choosing the permutation pair $(\sigma,\tau)$ generating a sufficiently large and suitably "generic" subgroup of $S_n$, together with a controlled degree of the associated torus cover, one produces origami curves whose Veech groups fail to contain any principal congruence subgroup $\Gamma(N)$ despite having level structure compatible with $N$. The key mechanism is a monodromy argument: the permutation representation $(\sigma, \tau)$ induces an action on the fiber of the covering map that can be arranged, via explicit combinatorial constructions, to have image in $S_n$ that is incompatible with the reduction map $SL(2,\mathbb{Z}) \to SL(2,\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z})$ acting on the same set. Consequently, the Veech group's image under reduction mod $N$ is a proper subgroup of what a congruence subgroup would require, and a counting argument comparing the index of the Veech group to the index of the corresponding congruence subgroup certifies non-congruence.

We further verify, using Euler characteristic computations on the associated origami curve together with the Riemann-Hurwitz formula, that these constructions can be realized for translation surfaces of every genus $g > 1$, with the number of squares $n$ growing suitably with $g$. This extends prior isolated examples (largely confined to low genus) to a uniform construction, establishing that the phenomenon of non-congruence Veech groups is not exceptional but generic across the moduli space of translation surfaces once $g > 1$. Our results reinforce the perspective that Veech groups, despite strong analogies with Fuchsian groups derived from arithmetic settings, generically escape the congruence subgroup property, paralleling analogous phenomena in the theory of dessins d'enfants and Belyi maps.
